newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Khmer Rouge supremo Pol Pot on run after killings.
newsitem.headline: Khmer Rouge supremo Pol Pot on run after killings.

text.p: Ailing Khmer Rouge supremo Pol Pot slaughtered his defence chief and 11 members of his family and fled his northern stronghold with a fellow leader of the Maoist movement as hostage, Cambodia's co-premier said on Friday.

Ageing Pol Pot, who led the Khmer Rouge during its brutal "killing fields" rule over Cambodia from 1975 to early 1979, was carried off by his men in a sling because he was too sick to move quickly, First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh told reporters.

"Mr Pol Pot had accused (defence chief) Son Sen of being allied with Second Prime Minister Hun Sen, so on the 10th of June at 2 a.m., he killed Son Sen and 11 of his family members very brutally, very cruelly, by shooting them and running over the dead with a truck," said Ranariddh.

Government officials said fighting broke out briefly on Friday at the stronghold in Anlong Veng between 200 hardliners loyal to Pol Pot and a breakaway group of nearly 2,000 other Khmer Rouge guerrillas believed to have defected to the Phnom Penh government.

After shooting his long-time comrade-in-arms and his family members, Pol Pot fled into nearby jungle with some loyalists, taking along as a hostage Khieu Samphan, a senior Khmer Rouge official seen as a frontman for the group.

Ranariddh did not say where Pol Pot, who is believed to be riddled with malaria, may have gone. Cambodia and Thailand both said they had sealed their borders to prevent him from escaping. Officials in Thailand vowed to help Phnom Penh capture Pol Pot, one of the 20th century's most notorious figures.
Ranariddh's announcement came amid persistent reports in recent days of conflict between Pol Pot, Son Sen and Khieu Samphan.
Khmer Rouge radio, which usually broadcasts in the mornings, fell silent on Friday.
Ranariddh and Hun Sen have been trying to woo breakaway Khmer Rouge rebels ahead of national elections expected to be held next year.
The guerrilla movement began unravelling last August when a senior rebel, Ieng Sary, broke with hardliners and eventually forged peace with the government.
Since then, thousands of rebels have defected to government ranks and fewer than 2,000 troops are thought to remain in Anlong Veng.
Khmer Rouge rebels, who reneged on a 1991 peace pact, have been fighting a low-intensity war against the Cambodian coalition government formed after U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993.

Pol Pot led the Khmer Rouge during its brutal rule over Cambodia when more than a million pople died from executions, starvation, sickness or overwork. He is wanted by the Cambodian government and the World Court on charges of genocide.
The fighting at Anlong Veng was reported by press department director Leng Sochea.
"This morning from 9 a.m. to 10 a.m., there was fighting between Khmer Rouge rebels... in Anlong Veng," he said.
General Long Sereyrath said government forces intercepted radio transmissions around Anlong Veng and that rebels were heard arguing over the radio and abusing each other.
After the clash, a group of fleeing fighters were identified as Pol Pot followers, a senior Cambodian military adviser said.
A division of about 2,000 government troops, including 600 former Khmer Rouge who had defected to the government several months ago, had been dispatched to the area, he said.
Pol Pot was rumoured earlier this week to have left Cambodia for Bangkok en route to political exile in China. Thai military sources and China denied this.
Ranariddh said he had photographs of the bodies of Son Sen and members of his family but did not say when he would release them.
"I have enough evidence with pictures to show the killing of Son Sen," the premier said.

Ranariddh did not say where or how he obtained the news of Son Sen's death and the photographs. But one of his senior military commanders returned on Thursday night from a trip to Anlong Veng where he was said to have met Khmer Rouge hardliners.
"I hope this is the end of the life of the Khmer Rouge really because Pol Pot cannot live any longer," he said.
Ranariddh said he had no information on the group's army commander, the one-legged Ta Mok.

"The immediate task for the Cambodian troops is to rescue Khieu Samphan and later join hands in crushing the remaining Khmer Rouge guerrillas led by the hardliner Pol Pot," said a Thai general who deals with the Cambodian conflict.
"Pol Pot would have no where to go but to die in Cambodia," the general said.
